No other label does (p7y.subdomain and frpc.subdomain are ignored). shell gets no TCP address: that name is the sandbox's own SSH (Shell and logs). p9m.access Who may open the address (App access). p9m.connect.user The login the Connect… recipes use (below). p9m.publish, p9m.title, p9m.description, p9m.image Lists the app on the Hub. 
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    labels:
      p9m.subdomain: web

A container with p9m.subdomain that publishes several ports has one web address for all of them; each port's TCP address (below) gets -port<N> too.

docs.title: TLS TCP addresses
docs.text:
A port an inner container publishes on all interfaces ("5432:5432") also gets a TCP address, its HTTP name plus -tcp, on port 443, TLS only: shop-inner-db-port5432-tcp.<domain>:443. Ports published on 127.0.0.1 stay private: no TCP address and no link.

  • Postgres: psql "host=shop-inner-db-port5432-tcp.<domain> port=443 sslmode=require …"
  • Any client that speaks TLS (Redis --tls, MQTTS): connect with that name as SNI.
  • SSH through TLS: ProxyCommand openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h.

Traefik passes these names through to Purgatorium's TCP gateway, which terminates TLS (with certs/tls.crt, or a self-signed *.<domain> kept in data/), wakes the sandbox if needed and connects to the sandbox container over traefik-net. There is no extra authentication: the service's own login protects it. Only web traffic keeps a sandbox awake: without it the sandbox sleeps after its idle timeout even with an open TCP connection, which then drops; the next connection wakes it. Right after a wake the service itself may still be starting (Postgres answers the database system is starting up), so let the client retry. The details panel lists the addresses with ready-made commands (Connect…), picked by the container's own port (5432 Postgres, 6379 Redis, 22 or 2222 SSH; anything else gets the generic TLS recipe). A p9m.connect.user label on the container puts its login into those commands. The API gives the same as tcp_addresses (address, port, user) next to tcp_urls.

The tcp-demo template (on either runtime) shows it end to end. Its starter stack has a Postgres with a sample orders table (<name>-db-tcp), a Redis (<name>-redis-tcp), an SSH server with the user demo (<name>-ssh-tcp) and pgweb in the browser (https://<name>-pgweb.<domain>, user demo), all behind one generated password (Demo password in the details panel and in Connect…). Insert a row with psql and it shows up in pgweb:

psql "host=<name>-db-tcp.<domain> port=443 sslmode=require user=postgres dbname=postgres" -c "insert into orders (customer, item, amount) values ('me', 'espresso', 3)"
redis-cli -h <name>-redis-tcp.<domain> -p 443 --tls --sni <name>-redis-tcp.<domain> -a <password> ping   # add --insecure with the self-signed certificate
ssh -o ProxyCommand="openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h" demo@<name>-ssh-tcp.<domain>

The three TCP containers also get an HTTP link in Apps (frpc tunnels every published port); those links do not lead anywhere useful.

docs.title: CPU and memory
docs.text:
Every sandbox runs with a CPU and memory limit: the sandbox and everything inside it share it (the inner containers live in the sandbox container's cgroup). New sandboxes get SANDBOX_CPUS / SANDBOX_MEMORY (default 2 CPUs, 4 GB); on create (Advanced) or later (Resources… in the panel, PATCH /sandboxes/:name with cpus, memory) a user can raise their sandbox's limits up to SANDBOX_MAX_CPUS / SANDBOX_MAX_MEMORY (default 4 and 8 GB), the admin up to the host's size. A change applies at once without a restart (docker update) and is kept in the sandbox's compose file. Memory below what a running sandbox uses now is refused (stop it first). There is no swap beyond the memory limit.

The panel shows the sandbox's current CPU and memory against its limits (sampled every 10 s), and the list a short CPU · Mem column for running sandboxes. The API gives limits (cpus, memory in bytes) and, for a running sandbox, usage (cpu in cores, memory, memory_limit).

docs.title: Disk
docs.text:
Everything a sandbox keeps (its inner images, containers and volumes) is in its own docker_data volume. Purgatorium measures it from outside with du: a running sandbox every 15 minutes, an asleep one once after it stopped (its size does not change while it sleeps); the results are kept in data/disk-usage.json. The Resources tab shows the use against the sandbox's disk limit, SANDBOX_DISK (20 GB by default); the admin can set another one per sandbox (Change limits…, or PATCH /sandboxes/:name with disk).

Above the limit the panel and the sandbox list show ⚠ and suggest cleaning up (docker system prune in the sandbox). It is only a warning: nothing is stopped or refused, and a sandbox can use more until the host's disk is full. A hard limit (a fixed-size disk per sandbox) is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Open, not yet scheduled
docs.text:
• Isolation between neighbouring sandboxes: published ports (foxglove image). Today this is Docker's usual behaviour: a port an inner container publishes on all interfaces (9000:9000, as the starter does) is reachable from every other sandbox on the DinD container's traefik-net address, protected only by the app's own login; 127.0.0.1:9000:9000 stays private (see Isolation between sandboxes). The frps API (:7500) has a password since 0.6, and the Docker API needs the sandbox's client certificate. To close published ports to neighbours: in the foxglove image (dind and sysbox), after dockerd starts, iptables -I DOCKER-USER -i eth+ -m conntrack ! --ctstate RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j DROP (and ip6tables); frpc connects from the inside, so the tunnels keep working. To work out:
  • Purgatorium's TCP gateway connects over traefik-net too: the rule would cut the -tcp addresses, SSH and Docker access unless Purgatorium's address is let through (it changes when Purgatorium is recreated; a fixed address on traefik-net, or a mark the rule can match);
  • sandboxes that are meant to talk to each other (one's app using another's database): opt in per sandbox, or through the TLS TCP addresses;
  • a new foxglove release for both runtimes, and existing sandboxes on it;
  • the "by design" check in tests/isolation.sh reversed.
  • A Kata Containers runtime, for untrusted code. Each sandbox in its own lightweight VM with its own kernel, so root inside a sandbox no longer means root on the host (today's dind runtime is privileged). Docker supports Kata through its containerd shim ("runtimes": {"kata": {"runtimeType": "io.containerd.kata.v2"}} in the host's daemon.json, then runtime: kata in the sandbox's compose service), so it fits next to dind and sysbox as a third runtime with the same wiring (FRP tunnel, Traefik route, Sablier, docker_data volume, archive). To work out:
  • the host needs hardware virtualization (KVM): bare metal, or a cloud VM with nested virtualization;
  • dockerd inside the Kata VM: privileged there applies to the VM only, not the host, but must not pass the host's devices through;
  • the docker_data volume and its performance (virtio-fs), and how the CPU and memory limits map to the VM's size;
  • a foxglove image for it, and the same integration tests as for the other runtimes;
  • still a sandbox (same API, lifecycle, quota and UI), with its isolation shown as a badge next to its name and chosen at create time ("Isolation: Container / MicroVM"): dind 🟠 privileged, sysbox 🔵 container, kata 🟢 microVM. "MicroVM" is said only where it is true: dind and sysbox sandboxes share the host's kernel.
  • GPUs in sandboxes. Today no sandbox sees a GPU. A sandbox could ask for one at create time, like CPUs and memory, and the list, the panel and the API would show which have one (a GPU column with the model, e.g. RTX 4090). It suits the sleep model: a sleeping sandbox could give its GPU back, and the next one to wake take it. To work out:
  • per runtime: dind needs the NVIDIA driver and nvidia-container-toolkit on the host, the device passed to the sandbox container and the toolkit in the foxglove image, so the inner Docker hands it on to the apps; whether and how sysbox (the production runtime) passes GPUs through, to check first; Kata only through VFIO, typically one GPU per VM;
  • detecting the host's GPUs at startup and in check-host.sh (nvidia-smi, Docker's runtimes);
  • limits and quota (SANDBOX_MAX_GPUS, the admin beyond), as for CPU and memory;
  • a whole GPU per sandbox, or shared (time-slicing, MIG);
  • what a waking sandbox does when every GPU is taken: wait, refuse, or start without one.
  • To review: every path into a sandbox through frp. Today there are two paths. Web addresses go Traefik → <name>-socat:8080 → frps → tunnel → frpc → app. TLS TCP addresses (-tcp), Docker access (-docker) and SSH (-shell-tcp) go Traefik (TLS passthrough) → Purgatorium's TCP gateway → straight to the sandbox container's port on traefik-net. The frp tunnel is the one to keep and extend: frpc connects out of the sandbox, so Purgatorium and Traefik never need to reach into it. That is what lets the same wiring carry sandboxes whose inside is not directly reachable: a microVM runtime (Kata, Firecracker), sandboxes on another machine or behind NAT, Kubernetes pods. The direct TCP path works for dind and sysbox on one host only. To work out:
  • TCP addresses, Docker access and SSH through frp as well (frp has TCP proxies, not only HTTP): frpc registers them like the web ports, and Purgatorium's TCP gateway keeps only what it is for (TLS for the -tcp names, waking, choosing the target), connecting to frps instead of the sandbox container;
  • what frps exposes for that (a port per TCP proxy, or frp's tcpmux/STCP) and how it stays unreachable from neighbouring sandboxes;
  • the TCP path still needs Purgatorium (its addresses do not answer while Purgatorium is down or upgrading, and open connections drop): whether Traefik could carry it with TCP routers to frps, which have no Sablier middleware;
  • one rule for staying awake on every path: traffic in the last minute, not an open connection (today: every web request; a -docker connection while bytes go through it, never waking a sleeping one, since Docker Desktop reconnects to every context at once; a -tcp connection not at all, though it wakes one);
  • moving existing sandboxes over; the Kata runtime and Kubernetes support build on this.
  • The Hub, next steps. The Hub lists the apps builders publish with a label. Still open: a webhook when an app is published (Slack, n8n, a Lemmy bot, without an RSS reader in between); a Hub per team, with Teams; a Hub open on the internal network without signing in, for small installs without single sign-on; p9m.publish.port to choose which of an app's ports it opens.
  • Deploy from git. Today a sandbox gets its apps through docker compose (the API, SSH, the Docker CLI or an agent). Next: connect a repository, and a push builds the image and deploys it into the sandbox, like a self-hosted Vercel; optionally a preview sandbox per branch or pull request, which sleeps like any other and is archived when the branch is merged. To work out:
  • where the build runs: in the sandbox's own Docker (its CPU and memory limits apply, and the image goes to the Purgatorium registry, which already scans pushes for secrets);
  • how Purgatorium reaches the repository and hears about pushes: a webhook from GitHub/GitLab/Gitea, or polling, and a deploy key per sandbox;
  • projects without a Dockerfile or a compose file: buildpacks (Nixpacks, Cloud Native Buildpacks), or refuse them with a clear message;
  • build logs in the panel and the API, and what a failed build does to the running version (it keeps running).
  • Teams: a sandbox owned by a group, so several people see and manage it, and other teams do not; optionally a quota per team.
  • A hard disk quota per sandbox. Today a sandbox above its disk limit is only flagged (see Disk). For a hard limit: its docker_data as a fixed-size ext4 image, loop-mounted through the local volume driver (type=ext4, o=loop); to work out: moving existing sandboxes' data, resizing (only while stopped), the archive, Docker Desktop. The Kata runtime gets this from its VM disk.
  • Kubernetes support: move the runtime layer behind the Docker-specific code; Sablier's Kubernetes provider helps here.

docs.title: Runtimes and templates
docs.text:
A sandbox is a runtime (how it runs) plus a template (what runs inside), picked separately on create (runtime, template; the New sandbox form has a select for each):

Runtime Isolation Use dind privileged: true development, any Docker host (incl. Docker Desktop / WSL) sysbox runtime: sysbox-runc, no privileged mode production; requires sysbox on a Linux host Template What runs inside starter (default) a hello app; deploy yours with docker, SSH or an agent portainer the same with Portainer, a web UI for the sandbox's Docker (its address and password in the API and the panel; it runs with -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock, so its environment exists from the start) tcp-demo a demo of TLS TCP addresses: Postgres, Redis, SSH and pgweb empty nothing: paste your own compose file in the dialog

Both runtimes have the same wiring (FRP tunnel, Traefik route, Sablier sleep/wake, docker_data volume, archive on delete). The sysbox image runs plain dockerd, so its TLS listener is configured through the runtime's daemon_json field, which Purgatorium merges into the generated daemon.json. Both run in production. On a shared server use sysbox only: install it on the host and set ALLOWED_RUNTIMES=sysbox (see Security).

Runtimes are runtimes/<name>.yaml: a description, the sandbox's own docker_compose (the DinD container, frps, socat, and their Traefik and Sablier labels) and an optional daemon_json. Templates are directories, templates/<name>/:

  • compose.yaml (required): the stack deployed into the sandbox's own Docker on creation, a plain compose file.
  • template.yaml (optional, every field optional): description (default: the directory name), before_script (JavaScript run on create; what it returns becomes ${variables} for both compose files and the sandbox's extras, e.g. a generated password), idle_timeout (Go duration, default 30m: how long a sandbox may go without HTTP traffic before it sleeps; a create request can override it), deep_sleep_after (default 7d), inner_project_name (default inner).

A new template is a new directory; it shows up in GET /templates and the form without a restart. In both files Purgatorium fills in ${name}, ${raw_name}, ${host_domain}, ${template_name}, ${runtime_name} and whatever before_script returned; any other ${…} is left for docker compose (write $$ for a literal $). Publish a port on all interfaces ("5432:5432") to give it a link and a TLS TCP address; a port on 127.0.0.1 stays private to the sandbox; a p9m.connect.user label puts its login into the Connect… commands. Pass passwords through variables whose name contains PASSWORD (or TOKEN, SECRET, KEY): Starter stack… masks those.

The New sandbox dialog shows the chosen template's compose.yaml; edit it there, or pick empty and paste your own (empty without a compose text is refused). The sandbox then gets that text (comments kept, the same variables filled in, the template's before_script still run) and shows "(edited)" in the list and its panel. The text is checked first: it must be YAML with at least one service, at most 256 KB, that docker compose accepts. Keys that would make the compose CLI (which runs in the Purgatorium container) read the server's files are refused: build, env_file, label_file, extends.file, include, and secrets/configs from a file or environment — build images through DOCKER_HOST or Portainer instead. The CLI gets no Purgatorium settings in its environment, so an unknown ${VAR} is empty.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Purgatorium is built for a team that trusts each other's intentions but not each other's mistakes: it keeps one person's broken compose file, runaway container or exposed port from affecting everyone else. It is not a boundary against hostile code.

What it does:

  • each user gets their own Docker daemon, so their containers, images, volumes and networks are separate from everyone else's and from the host's Docker;
  • an app's private addresses are reachable only inside its own sandbox, and ports published on 127.0.0.1 only through its tunnel (see Isolation between sandboxes);
  • users see and change only their own sandboxes, through the UI, the API or a personal access token; the admin sees all;
  • with an https:// PUBLIC_URL, Purgatorium refuses to start with default secrets.

On a shared server (several people, or agents running code you have not read): install sysbox on the host and set ALLOWED_RUNTIMES=sysbox in .env. New sandboxes then always run under sysbox, nobody can create a privileged dind one, and check-host.sh tells whether sysbox works on the machine. Sandboxes that already exist keep their runtime: recreate the dind ones.

What it does not do:

  • Without sysbox, sandboxes run privileged (the dind runtime). Code with root inside such a sandbox can escape to the host. By default (DEFAULT_RUNTIME=auto) new sandboxes use the sysbox runtime wherever sysbox is installed on the (Linux) host, which runs Docker in an unprivileged container; Docker Desktop cannot run sysbox, so there they fall back to dind, and Purgatorium says so at startup. Only let people and agents you would give a shell on the host run code in dind sandboxes.
  • sysbox is not a VM: its sandboxes run unprivileged, in their own user namespace, but share the host's kernel, so a kernel exploit would still reach the host.
  • There is no network policy between a sandbox and the internet, and no hard disk quota per sandbox: only a warning above its disk limit (see Disk); CPU and memory limits exist (see CPU and memory).
  • The Purgatorium container mounts the host's Docker socket, so whoever controls Purgatorium controls the host.
  • A host folder the admin mounts into a sandbox (HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS) is the sandbox owner's, as root, and every app's and agent's in it: read-only only limits writing. Keep the roots narrow.

For untrusted code (public sign-up, code from strangers), use sysbox or a microVM-based sandbox instead; a Kata Containers runtime (a VM per sandbox) is on the roadmap.

Found a vulnerability? See SECURITY.md.

docs.title: SSH into a sandbox
docs.text:
Every sandbox runs an sshd: root, keys only, at <name>-shell-tcp.<domain>:443 (the same TLS gateway as the TCP addresses). Add your public keys under SSH keys (/settings/ssh-keys, API GET/POST/DELETE /ssh-keys): they let you into all your sandboxes, and a change takes effect at once. A create request can add keys for that sandbox only (ssh_keys, or Advanced → Extra SSH public keys). Inside, docker talks to the sandbox's own Docker.

ssh -o ProxyCommand="openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h" root@<name>-shell-tcp.<domain>

Each new sandbox also has a key of its own: Download key in its panel (API GET /sandboxes/:name/ssh-key; POST makes one for an SSH sandbox that has none yet), so nobody has to make or upload a key first. The Connect… recipe then reads ssh -i ~/Downloads/<name>.key ….

The name shell is reserved: an inner service with p9m.subdomain: shell gets no TCP address.

docs.title: Terminal in the browser
docs.text: Terminal in a sandbox's panel opens a root shell in the sandbox in a new tab: nothing to install, no key. It wakes the sandbox if it is asleep, and keeps it awake while the tab is open. Inside, docker talks to the sandbox's own Docker. Only the sandbox's owner (and the admin) can open it, from the Purgatorium pages themselves (signed in; not with a token); at most 5 at once per user.

docs.title: App logs
docs.text: Logs in a sandbox's panel opens, in a new tab, what the apps in the sandbox write: the last 100 lines of every container (time, service name; errors in red), then new lines as they come. A filter shows one service; Pause holds new lines, Clear empties the view. It does not wake the sandbox or keep it awake: a sleeping one says asleep with a Start button. With a token: curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://p9m.example.com/sandboxes/p9m-shop/logs/stream. At most 5 viewers per sandbox at once.

docs.title: Sleep and wake
docs.text:
A sandbox is running, asleep (containers stopped, data intact), in deep sleep (containers and network removed, data intact) or archived (after an explicit delete). There is no fixed-time expiry: a sandbox only sleeps when nobody uses it, and only a person deleting it removes it.

Handled entirely by Sablier. The sandbox's outer containers (DinD, frps, socat) form one Sablier group and its Traefik router carries the Sablier middleware. After idle_timeout without HTTP traffic the group is stopped — which stops everything inside the sandbox too. The sandbox's router exists only while it runs, so the next request reaches Purgatorium's catch-all /wake, which wakes it within the owner's limits (see Web UI and sign-in) and shows a waiting page until the router is back; the socat healthcheck only passes once the FRP tunnel is online. Sablier still measures the idle time and puts the sandbox to sleep. Reset next to Sleeps in in the panel (POST /sandboxes/:name/keep-awake) starts the countdown over, as a visit would; it does not wake a sleeping sandbox.

Apps must set a restart policy to come back after sleep. When the sandbox wakes, its inner Docker daemon only restarts containers with restart: unless-stopped or restart: always. Without one, the app stays stopped and has to be started by hand (docker start, or from Portainer):

services:
  web:
    image: my-app
    restart: unless-stopped
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    restart: unless-stopped

HTTP traffic through Traefik counts as activity, and so does traffic on a Docker connection (DOCKER_HOST=tcp://<raw>-docker.<domain>:443): Purgatorium renews the session once a minute while bytes go through it. A Docker connection that is only open does not count, and a Docker connection never wakes a sleeping sandbox: Docker Desktop keeps every context connected for its Builds view and reconnects at once, so it would wake the sandbox each time it fell asleep. Wake it first (Wake, POST /sandboxes/:name/start, or open one of its apps); until then docker cannot connect. Sablier persists its sessions (--storage.file), so restarting Sablier does not put running sandboxes to sleep. A sandbox started without Purgatorium (Docker restarting it, docker compose start by hand, or Purgatorium restarted while it was starting one) has no session at first; Purgatorium notices within two minutes and opens one, so it still sleeps after its idle_timeout. After a host reboot, sandboxes that were asleep stay asleep.

The sandbox list (GET /sandboxes adds stops_at, deep_sleep_at and deep_sleep_after to each row) and the details panel show Sleeps in (time until Sablier stops a running sandbox; every request resets it — read from Sablier's /metrics, which Purgatorium reaches on sablier-net) and Deep sleep in (time until an asleep sandbox is taken down).

Both times can be changed after creation — Change… next to Sleep on the panel's Details tab, or PATCH /sandboxes/<name> with {"idle_timeout": "45m", "deep_sleep_after": "14d"} (either field; same formats as at creation; owner or admin). The values are written into the sandbox's docker-compose.yml. A new idle_timeout recreates only the socat container, which carries the Sablier middleware labels: a running sandbox's apps are unreachable for a few seconds, an asleep one stays asleep, and the DinD container and its inner stack are not touched; it applies from the next request's Sablier session. A new deep_sleep_after applies immediately — Purgatorium reads it from the compose file.

idle_timeout takes seconds, minutes, hours or days (30s, 30m, 2h, 1d); days are kept as hours (1d becomes 24h), because Sablier's durations have no days. deep_sleep_after takes m, h or d. The server can set a ceiling for users' sandboxes: SANDBOX_MAX_IDLE_TIMEOUT and SANDBOX_MAX_DEEP_SLEEP_AFTER (Configuration); a value above it, or never, is refused (at most 2h on this server). 0 or off means never, for both — at creation and when changing them. deep_sleep_after: off never takes the sandbox down. Sablier has no "never", so idle_timeout: off is written as a 10-year session (87600h): the sandbox keeps running, and if it is stopped by hand the next request still wakes it. The panel and the list show "never" for either.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
To a new version, in the install directory:

curl -fsSLO https://github.com/csakaszamok/p9m/releases/latest/download/docker-compose.yml
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d

If .env sets P9M_VERSION, change or remove it. Each release's notes are in the changelog.

docs.title: From Purgatory (p7y)
docs.text: There is no upgrade from Purgatory (p7y), the project's former name: install Purgatorium afresh, in a new directory called p9m. Nothing is carried over: sandboxes, archives, users, tokens and settings start empty, and P7Y_* settings and p7y.* labels are not read.

docs.title: Web UI and sign-in
docs.text:
Purgatorium has a small web UI (http://p9m.<HOST_DOMAIN>) for creating and managing sandboxes without the API directly, alongside the REST API.

Two ways to sign in:

  • Admin: a local account, set via ADMIN_USER / ADMIN_PASSWORD. Signs in with the "Administrator sign-in" form and sees every sandbox (My sandboxes + All sandboxes).
  • Everyone else: OIDC (Google or any OpenID Connect provider). Configure OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET and register the redirect URI $PUBLIC_URL/auth/callback with the provider — character for character (scheme, no trailing slash), under Google's Authorized redirect URIs, otherwise sign-in fails with redirect_uri_mismatch. Google accepts http:// redirect URIs only for localhost, so with Google use an https:// PUBLIC_URL (locally: a self-signed *.lvh.me certificate in certs/ and PUBLIC_URL=https://p9m.lvh.me, see HTTPS). OIDC_PROVIDER_NAME labels the sign-in button (default Google). Signed-in users only see their own sandboxes.

SESSION_SECRET signs the session cookie — set it to a long random string; sessions issued under an old value stop working if it changes.

Anyone with an account at the OIDC provider can sign in and create sandboxes, unless OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS or OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS limits it (e.g. to example.com): with Google, set one of them, or any Google account gets in. An account not on the list is told so on the sign-in page; one taken off the list is signed out, and its tokens stop working, once Purgatorium restarts with the new list. Each user may have SANDBOX_QUOTA sandboxes running at once (default 3, 0 = unlimited), guaranteed, and with SANDBOX_QUOTA_MAX more while the server has room to spare for the others' guarantees (Running 4 / 3 · up to 10 beside New sandbox); asleep, deep-sleeping and archived ones are not counted, so letting a sandbox sleep frees its place, and the admin is not limited. At the limit a user can neither create a sandbox nor wake one, from sleep or deep sleep: its address shows Running limit reached, its address shows Running limit reached with the running sandboxes, and Wake in the panel lets the owner put one to sleep instead (POST /sandboxes/:name/start with {"sleep": "<name>"}). Purgatorium never puts a sandbox to sleep on its own. Running sandboxes' web addresses do not go through Purgatorium: they keep working while it is down; waking needs it, and so do the TLS TCP addresses and Docker access (they go through Purgatorium's TCP gateway). SANDBOX_MAX_TOTAL (default 200) caps the running sandboxes on the whole server, the admin's included (asleep ones take no place): when it is reached nobody but the admin can create one or wake one (The server is full). The sign-in page shows the sandbox places above the sign-in buttons (taken and free; LOGIN_CAPACITY=off hides them), and once signed in the top bar does, on every page (e.g. 142 / 200 places, the free ones on hover; orange from 90%, red when full). The Overview page shows the counts as cards: running of how many allowed, asleep, deep sleep and archived; for the admin the sandbox places used against the server limit (the admin's own sandboxes take places too), the host's CPU and memory (used now and reserved by running sandboxes), the disk use, a table per owner and a Users table. Users lists every account that has signed in (by e-mail; admin for the local admin): when it was last seen (a page load, at most every 10 minutes), its last sign-in and how many, its sandboxes now and created, and its last API use (its tokens); no sandbox yet marks someone who signed in but never created one. The rows are kept in data/user-stats.json until the admin deletes one (Delete: only the row; the account and its sandboxes stay). Only the admin sees them (GET /users, DELETE /users/:account).

From Access tokens (/settings/tokens), a signed-in user can mint a personal access token (p9m_…) for their own agents to use as Authorization: Bearer p9m_…; the token acts as that user for the API. The full token is shown once, at creation. Tokens can be set to expire in 30 days, 90 days, or never, and can be revoked at any time.

A token can also be limited to one sandbox (Access in the dialog, or Token for this sandbox… on a sandbox panel's Access tab). Such a token lists and opens only that sandbox, and can start, stop and restart it and change its sleep times; it cannot create or delete sandboxes or manage tokens (403), and any other sandbox answers 404. Deleting the sandbox leaves the token in place: if you restore the sandbox, it works again.

With such a token an agent can deploy and update apps in the user's sandbox: the Purgatorium API gives it the sandbox's Docker client certificates, and the docker command line reaches the sandbox's own Docker daemon (or, in a sandbox from the portainer template, the Portainer API). Step by step: agent guide.

docs.title: Simple and Advanced
docs.text: The top bar has a Simple | Advanced switch, remembered for each account (users start in Simple, the admin in Advanced). Users have it only with USER_VIEW_SWITCH=true; by default they stay in Simple, see Configuration. Simple is for people who only want their app online: the menu shows My sandboxes only; the list shows the name, status, Sleeps in and age; a new sandbox asks for a name and a template; a sandbox panel has Wake or Sleep, an Apps tab (the web address of each app and Let your agent deploy…: the Claude Code plugin or a zip for other agents, the same window as in Advanced, which adds its Options) and a Details tab (when it last ran, the sleep times, warnings, archiving). Advanced shows everything: Overview, tokens, SSH keys, the Terminal and Logs, and the Access, Files, Resources and Registry tabs. Simple only hides: what an account may do is the same in both, and the API and MCP do not change. PUT /me/view with {"view": "simple"} or {"view": "advanced"} sets it (403 for a user without USER_VIEW_SWITCH=true); GET /me returns it as view, and whether the account may switch as view_switch.

docs.title: Host folders
docs.text:
The admin can mount folders of the host into a sandbox, e.g. a shared data folder, when HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS lists where they may come from (e.g. HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS=/srv/shared; see Configuration). On a sandbox panel's Resources tab, Host folders lists them, with Remove for each, and a form to add one: the host folder (at or under one of the roots), where it appears in the sandbox (empty: /mnt/<last part of the host path>) and read-only. The folder is bind-mounted into the sandbox container, so the apps in the sandbox's own Docker can bind it from there too (e.g. /mnt/shared:/data).

Adding or removing one recreates the sandbox container, after a confirmation: a running sandbox restarts (its apps are unreachable for a few seconds), an asleep one stays asleep, one in deep sleep gets the change when it wakes. A host folder that does not exist is not created: Docker refuses it, the panel shows Docker's message and nothing changes. The target cannot be /, a system directory (/etc, /usr, /proc, /dev, /run…) or on, above or under one of the sandbox's own mounts (/var/lib/docker, /opt, /root, /home, /srv, …). The mounts are kept in the sandbox's compose file (and its p9m.mounts label), so they survive sleep, deep sleep and upgrades.

A mount gives whoever owns the sandbox that host folder, as root, and every app and agent in it: mount read-only what they need not change, and only what they may see. The owner sees the list on the Resources tab, in Simple on Details (read-only); only the admin adds or removes them. With HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS unset no mount can be added; ones already there stay until the admin removes them. API: GET, POST and DELETE /sandboxes/:name/mounts (see API), over MCP list_sandbox_mounts, add_sandbox_mount and remove_sandbox_mount.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Step by step, from nothing to an app with a link you can send to anyone. No server knowledge needed: your coding agent does the technical part.

  • Put your app online with Claude Code: install the p9m plugin once, approve each project in the browser, then say deploy this app. The easiest way.
  • Put your app online with any agent: Codex, Cursor, or Claude Code without the plugin, with a zip from Purgatorium.
  • Share your app with your team on the Hub: list it where colleagues find, open and vote for it.

You need a Purgatorium account: the address your team uses (for example https://p9m.example.com) and a sign-in. Someone in your team set Purgatorium up; to set up your own, see Install.

docs.title: Put your app online with Claude Code
docs.text:
You have an app on your computer (a website, a dashboard, a small tool) and you want a link to it that works for anyone. Claude Code builds and runs it in your Purgatorium sandbox and gives you that link.

What you need: Claude Code (in a terminal, or the Code tab of the Claude desktop app), Docker installed on your computer, and a Purgatorium account.

docs.title: 1. Make a sandbox
docs.text:
1. Open your Purgatorium address in the browser and sign in.

  2. Click + New sandbox, give it a short name (for example shop), keep the template and click Create. It takes 10–30 seconds.

A sandbox is your own small server: your app runs there, not on your computer.

Simple or Advanced

The switch at the top right changes how much the screen shows. Simple is enough for everything here. If you see no switch, you are in Simple: the server lets only the admin switch.

docs.title: 2. Install the p9m plugin in Claude Code (once)
docs.text:
1. In Purgatorium, click your sandbox, then Let your agent deploy….

  2. In the window's step 1, click Copy next to each of the two lines, open a terminal (in VS Code: Terminal → New Terminal; on Windows also PowerShell, on a Mac the Terminal app), paste them one after the other and press Enter after each:

    claude plugin marketplace add csakaszamok/p9m
claude plugin install p9m@p9m

    It installs the plugin for you, in all your projects. It asks for no address and no token.

Good to know

  • claude not found? Claude Code is not installed for the terminal: see Claude Code's setup. An unknown option means an older Claude Code: run claude update.
  • Already in Claude Code? In Claude Code instead in the same window shows the same two lines as /plugin marketplace add csakaszamok/p9m and /plugin install p9m@p9m. (The Claude Code panel in VS Code has no /plugin: use the terminal.)

You install the plugin once. Each project then gets its sandbox in the next step.

docs.title: 3. Connect your project folder to the sandbox (once per folder)
docs.text:
Claude Code needs to know which sandbox belongs to which folder. You tell it once per folder; after that it remembers.

  1. Open your app's folder in Claude Code: start claude in that folder, or open the folder in VS Code or the desktop app.

  2. In Purgatorium, in the Let your agent deploy… window, step 2, click Copy. Paste the line into Claude Code and press Enter. It looks like this, with your Purgatorium's address and your sandbox's name:

    /p9m:init https://p9m.example.com shop

  3. Claude Code answers with a link and a code, for example:

    Open https://p9m.example.com/activate?code=TGMH-BSGQ and approve the code TGMH-BSGQ.

  4. Open the link in your browser (sign in if Purgatorium asks). The page shows the code and the sandbox. Check that the code is the same one Claude Code printed, then click Approve.

  5. Go back to Claude Code. Within a few seconds it says the folder is connected to the sandbox. That is all.

Approve only your own code

Approve a code only if you just ran /p9m:init yourself and Claude Code shows that same code. If someone sends you a link like this, do not approve it: whoever started that code would get into your sandbox. Click Deny instead.

What happened behind the scenes: Claude Code got a token for this one sandbox and the sandbox's Docker keys, and wrote them into a .p9m folder in your project. You never see or copy them. The folder is secret, and it keeps itself out of git on its own: leave it there. The token works for 90 days (then run /p9m:init again). You can revoke it in Purgatorium: Advanced → Access tokens, where it is named Claude Code init <date>.

If something goes wrong

  • The code ran out: it works for 10 minutes and only once. Run the same /p9m:init line again for a new code.
  • You clicked Deny by mistake: run /p9m:init again.
  • The button says Enable Docker access and approve: the sandbox does not let Docker in yet. Click it: the sandbox restarts (about 30 seconds) and Claude Code carries on by itself.
  • The folder was connected to another sandbox already: Claude Code asks before it replaces that connection.
  • A wrong sandbox in the list: if the line names a sandbox that is not yours, the page lets you pick one of your own sandboxes instead.

docs.title: 4. Deploy
docs.text:
In the same folder, say in your own words:

Deploy this app.

Claude Code wakes the sandbox, builds your app there, starts it and checks that it answers. At the end it gives you a link like https://shop-web.example.com (your sandbox's name first). Open it: that is your app, and it works for anyone you send it to.

docs.title: 5. Change and update
docs.text:
Changed something? Say:

Update the app.

The same link shows the new version a few seconds later.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Sleep: when nobody uses the app for a while (30 minutes by default), the sandbox sleeps to free the server. The next visit wakes it in a few seconds: the visitor sees waking up and then your app. Nothing is lost.
  • Sleep later: let it sleep only after 2 hours without visitors works too, or set it in Purgatorium: the sandbox → Details → Sleep → Change… (never is there as well).
  • It does not answer? Ask Claude Code why does my app not answer?: it reads the app's logs in the sandbox. The usual cause is an app that listens only on localhost; Claude Code fixes that.
  • Only for you or your colleagues? Say make it visible only to me (or only to my colleagues): Claude Code sets p9m.access (App access), and opening the link then asks the visitor to sign in to Purgatorium.
  • Docker is needed on your computer only for its command line: the build runs in the sandbox.

docs.title: More projects
docs.text:
Each folder is tied to one sandbox by its own .p9m folder, so different folders can use different sandboxes, even on different Purgatorium servers. For another folder, do step 3 there: in Purgatorium, on that folder's sandbox, Let your agent deploy…, copy the /p9m:init line and paste it into Claude Code in that folder. The plugin needs no new setup.

To move a folder to another sandbox, run that sandbox's /p9m:init line in the folder: Claude Code asks, then replaces the connection.

Used the earlier plugin, which asked for an address and a token? Run /plugin marketplace update p9m once, then /p9m:init in each project.

More details: Claude Code plugin.

docs.title: Share your app with your team on the Hub
docs.text:
The Hub is your team's showcase: a page at https://hub.<your Purgatorium domain> where colleagues find the apps you published, open them with one click, and vote for the ones they like. Colleagues who only use apps can sign in to the Hub alone.

What you need: an app already online in your sandbox (see Put your app online with Claude Code), and the Hub turned on in your Purgatorium (ask whoever runs it; it is HUB_ENABLED=true).

docs.title: 1. Publish
docs.text:
Tell your agent:

Publish the web app on the Hub, titled "Stock room", described as "Who took what from the stock room".

It adds labels to the app's service in its compose file and deploys again:

services:
  web:
    labels:
      p9m.publish: "true"
      p9m.title: "Stock room"
      p9m.description: "Who took what from the stock room"

Within about a minute and a half the app is on the Hub. In Purgatorium its Apps tab marks it On the Hub.

docs.title: 2. A picture on its card
docs.text:
Use /screenshot.png as its Hub image.

That adds p9m.image: "/screenshot.png": a picture the app itself serves (PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF, up to 2 MB). Without it the Hub uses the page's own preview image, if it has one, or the title's first letter.

docs.title: 3. Share
docs.text:
Send colleagues the Hub's address. They see whether your app is running or asleep; Open wakes it if it sleeps. Everyone signed in can vote once for each app, yours too.

To take it off the Hub: remove the app from the Hub (the agent removes p9m.publish), or archive the sandbox.

All labels and settings: Hub.

docs.title: Put your app online with any agent
docs.text:
For Codex, Cursor, Claude Code without the plugin, or any agent that can run commands on your computer. You download a small zip from Purgatorium; the agent uses it to build and run your app in your sandbox, and gives you its link.

What you need: the agent, Docker installed on your computer, and a Purgatorium account with a sandbox (+ New sandbox in Purgatorium; see step 1 of the Claude Code tutorial).

docs.title: 1. Download the zip
docs.text:
In Purgatorium, click your sandbox, then Let your agent deploy… → Download; in the Advanced view the same window also has Options (the token's name and expiry, a zip without the Docker keys, Copy as .env). You get p9m-<sandbox>.zip.

It holds a token for this sandbox and its keys: treat it like a password. Do not email it or commit it.

docs.title: 2. Hand it to the agent
docs.text:
Open your app's folder with the agent and say:

Set up the p9m zip from my Downloads in this project and deploy.

The agent unpacks it into a .p9m folder in your project, deletes the zip, builds your app in the sandbox, starts it and gives you its link. The .p9m folder keeps itself out of git on its own (it has its own .gitignore); leave it there, the agent uses it for every later update.

If the agent does not know what to do, point it to the instructions inside: read .p9m/README.md and deploy this app to my sandbox.

docs.title: 3. Update
docs.text: Changed something? Update the app in my sandbox. The same link shows the new version.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The zip's token expires in 90 days (in the Advanced view you can choose 30 days or never). Download a new zip then.
  • Lost the zip, or someone else got it? In Purgatorium (Advanced view): the sandbox → Access → Rotate Docker keys… makes the old keys useless, and Access tokens lets you revoke its token.
  • Sleep and wake work the same as with Claude Code: see Good to know there.

For agent builders: everything the agent does is in the agent guide.
